headphone-wireless-sony-wh-ch510.review: Not bad sound: balanced-warm. On-ear fit, good for sports. Outside noise still gets in. Decent microphone. No ANC. A wireless headphone that simply does the job, but the sound really is decent, balanced.

headphone-wireless-jbl510bt.review: Just buy the Sony CH520; this is half-baked. JBL is overpriced without many features. Such a shame. NOT SPONSORED: I've tried both. Sony has the bigger battery and custom EQ app support. Or get the Edifier W800BT Plus.

headphone-wireless-pioneer-se-s3bt.review: Very muffled. Such a shame, bro. Better than Lenovo, but still very muffled. The cushions are really hard and tight. Save up a bit more, bro: get the Edifier W800BT Plus or Sony CH520.

headphone-wireless-baseus-h1i.review: Sounds like a phone loudspeaker pressed to your ear: no lows, no highs, all mids. 100-hour battery, 38 ms gaming mode, custom EQ, ANC. The features are actually good; the sound is just rubbish.

headphone-wireless-lenovo-thinkplus.review: Muffled, weird and unclear; the mic is unclear too. It's like a speaker covered with a carpet: that muffled. Don't fall for cheap TikTok stuff. If you don't have the budget, don't just want to look like an influencer wearing an expensive wireless headphone like the AirPods Max around your neck and end up buying something like this. Think about the FUNCTION. If you really need a good mic and good sound that isn't muffled and weird like this, just buy a WIRED one like the Edifier K800: really nice, cheaper than this, and clearly functional. Don't fall for the social pressure to own a cheap wireless headphone.

headphone-focal-clear-mg.review: Hands down, the best headphone on Earth for me. The frequency graph leans neutral, the bass even slopes down, yet damn, the bass is still impactful. Clear across all frequencies. Best of all, the positioning in height, depth and left-right: oh, so different. The room acoustics are insanely good. Enjoyable timbre: warm, but with godly separation and imaging. And the sound doesn't try to be weird or different: neutral, warm, in line with every other pro audio brand.

headphone-hifiman-edition-xv.review: FINALLY A HIFIMAN THAT DOESN'T SOUND BRIGHT AND THIN ANY MORE! The graph is really great, mate: the mid-bass isn't high, it runs perfectly straight down into the sub-bass, and the upper mids aren't as high as the Audeze MM100. So it's just more balanced. It's neutral, but the neutral headphones on the market so far roll off from the mid-bass to the sub; this doesn't, it's straight. You save money and I'd say it's even better than some Arya models, with very high value for money. Pair this with a Topping DX5 and you're done. More than enough, really.

headphone-audeze-mm100.review: Wowww, finally a planar I like, compared with HiFiMan, even ones under 20 million rupiah. Tuned by sound engineer Manny Marroquin. Spacious, lovely vocals, deep, well-delivered sub-bass, not thin at all, with just the right quantity and punch. Not over-exciting, not too boring-neutral: really, really good. If the song is exciting, it's exciting; if the song is flat and neutral, it delivers that well too. Better than the Sundara, Ananda and Edition XS.

headphone-sennheiser-hd650.review: This is the industry standard for mixing. Natural timbre, and more correct than the HD600: more musical, more enjoyable, safer treble, and smoooother. Sennheiser's HD650 open-back really is very natural. You won't go wrong with the HD600, HD650 or HD58X; only the HD660S I don't like. Weird. (Review on his YouTube.)

headphone-sennheiser-hd600.review: The industry standard for mixing and audiophiles since 1994. You can hear mixing mistakes and shortcomings on it. Excellent. If you're not used to a neutral headphone like this, the bass will feel lacking, but you get to HEAR WHAT THE AUDIO ENGINEER WANTS YOU TO HEAR: listen to the music exactly the way the mixing engineer wants you to hear it. Enjoyably vocal-centric too. The soundstage is narrower than the HD650. TRUST ME, many audiophiles and audio engineers agree: these HD-series headphones are better than other headphones that even cost $2,000. (Review on his YouTube.)

headphone-audio-technica-r70x.review: Lots of people like this, and it's good. I just don't love the treble and the driver resolution: to me the driver timbre isn't as clear, accurate and studio-monitor-like as the HD650 and HD600. I'm still very much holding on to my 650. But I can see why some people love this as well. The fit is OK too; I slightly prefer Sennheiser's fit, especially with ZMF earpads. For some people it's in the same class as the HD6 series.

headphone-sennheiser-hd550.review: The best HD5xx model, the tuning I like most compared with the 505 and HD560S. The price could be a bit lower; maybe 3–4 million rupiah would suit it better. The highs are a little safer than the 505 or ATH-R50x. Intimate vocals, very close and in front. The best tonality, maybe even more balanced than the HD650; it just loses on resolution and separation against the HD6xx drivers.

headphone-audio-technica-r50x.review: Wow, this is really lovely. Compared with the HD560S it has more air, but the fit is much nicer: less swivel trouble, and although the earcups are a bit smaller than the HD560S, for some reason it's just more comfortable: the curve of the pad material, and better headband padding too. This sits below the R70x. Imaging and soundstage are very OK for such a low price. Definitely a very good product. Maybe a bit dark in the upper mids around 3 kHz, but lots of air treble at the top of the presence. Still similar to the R70x, with a more forgiving 8 kHz but a slightly brighter treble on average.

headphone-sennheiser-hd560s.review: Wow, this is sooooo goooood. More bass, not boosted: still neutral but you feel the kick. Good for mixing too; having bass doesn't mean boosted. Transparent, grand, mid-centric, very Sennheiser. Value for money if you can't get an HD650 or HD660. By far a better alternative to buying the HD58X. Clear, detailed, grand. Nice earpads too.

headphone-sennheiser-hd58x.review: If you want to start buying Sennheiser's HD series, well, this is it. The HD58X, HD600, HD650 and HD660S are much more ALIKE than they are DIFFERENT; they feel similar, not far apart. So for value for money you can buy this one. It's the fun one: more bass, slightly less treble. Great for loud songs with wide guitar panning. Very enjoyable.

headphone-sennheiser-hd620s.review: Very neutral, better clarity, and a more open soundstage. Downsides: the fit keeps shifting when I wear it, and it's overpriced for closed-back monitors; all of this can be had from the K361, DT770, even the FiiO FT1, or eveeen the HD280 Pro in the same pro line-up. Only the fit and clamp are roomier than the HD280.

headphone-sennheiser-hd505.review: A crazy price, though the dollar is crazy too right now. More or less similar to the HD560S, just warmer, and with more low end compared with the HD6 series. Not that impressed. I haven't tried the 550 yet; foreign reviewers say it's better. Between this and the 560S, I still prefer the 560S, especially at its very sexy price of just over 3 million.

headphone-fiio-ft1.review: This is really good. It challenges other monitoring headphones like the Beyer DT770, M50x, MDR-7506, or even the Sennheiser HD620S Closed. Very balanced and tidy; good imaging, good, natural timbre. Cool mesh pads, big earcups. Very comfortable for session players monitoring a recording. Deep bass, extended but not overdone/boomy. Sparkly treble, a bit dangerous at 5 kHz; very loud it gets a bit bright. Detachable cable, comes with a nice case.

headphone-beyerdynamic-dt770-pro.review: Beyerdynamic's most legendary closed-back headphone, since 1985. Watch any BBC Radio 1 Live Lounge video on YouTube, or radio DJs in the studio: they all still use this. Truly the industry-standard closed-back. Flat, but with a bit of boost in the low and high end, so it's fun for instruments too. And if you play in a band, monitoring on this is damn excellent. Wide staging. Closed-backs are hard to make because you need an acoustic space behind the driver, and this is one of the best out there. A must; many even use it to play Valorant.

headphone-sennheiser-hd280-pro.review: A good one from Sennheiser. I think the best sound at around 2 million rupiah is this and the K361: the most accurate timbre and sound for reproducing what you record into the DAW. The soundstage is fairly spacious too, and no frequency is too bright. Weaknesses: not detachable (maybe moddable at Guiltorin), and the earpads flake like the MDR-7506's. But this is more than enough compared with the HD620S.

headphone-akg-k361.review: AKG's best headphone, in my view, under 3 million rupiah. Good neutrality: better than the Beyer DT770 Pro on neutrality and accuracy, and better than the M50x, MDR-7506 and SRH440A. Really good. A clear, clean midrange. Comfortable too, and detachable.

headphone-shure-srh840a.review: Lovely. More clarity than the SRH440, with brighter mids too. Pleasant, and the price has dropped. Very sturdy build quality. Very OK. Only at high volume it can get bright, same as the DT770. If you want good build, good sound and a price not as high as Beyer, this is an attractive option.

headphone-sony-mdr-7506.review: Sony's most legendary professional headphone, since 1991, still made ONLY in Japan. Used for recording monitoring and TV/radio broadcasting. The tuning is boosted quite a lot in the upper mids/treble, but that makes it good for monitoring human voices and mixing mistakes. Yet music is also more fun on it than on any other headphone at the same price. ALL PARTS ARE SERVICEABLE, and many people still mod it to be detachable, swap earpads, headbands etc. Better build quality than the ATH-M50x and M40x.

headphone-shure-srh440a.review: Neutral. I prefer this to the bassy M50x. An enjoyable neutral sound, and the comfort is very OK; compared with the DT770 Pro, this may be the better pick for comfort.

headphone-hifiman-sundara.review: If you want to buy a planar, at least get this, not the HE400. You feel the planar character here: fast, of course, and distorted and acoustic guitars sound MEATIER! Excellent, like playing a Telecaster with a Tube Screamer overdrive switched on. Twangy. But as an all-rounder I'd still pick the HD650 over this, because your mixing becomes less accurate when you hear everything with the planar's fast transients and clear top end. That's it. The bass is also more present than the HD600.

headphone-aune-sr7000.review: Still neutral, a bit more open-sounding than the AR5000, and fuller-sounding too. Sadly nothing impresses me that much. At this price point I'd much prefer the Audeze MM100.

headphone-aune-ar5000.review: OK. Dead neutral and boring. My preference is still the HD600/650 if you can save up, or I'd pick a closed-back like the DT770 or similar. The sub-bass isn't extended enough; not because it isn't boosted, it's just too lacking and not thick enough, IMO. Not open enough, a bit blunt. On the graph it looks fine. I'll pick the big German brand any day.

headphone-sony-mdr-mv1.review: A bit bright in the lower treble; I don't like it much. The sound is open, like most open-backs, but very bright. My advice: the HD560S instead.

headphone-fiio-jt7.review: A more neutral tonality, with safer treble at 8 kHz than the JT3. The mids are still fairly high around 2–3 kHz. It folds. Cleaner bass. Comes with 2 cables, including 4.4 mm. My advice is the same dilemma for 1-million headphones: if I recommend a desktop DAC/amp, it'll be 3–5 million, like the DX5 II. If you just want to try it, a SnowSky Melody still works, and you get EQ and enough loudness, but the technical fullness and sense of space won't match a desktop DAC/amp. But give it a try: it's cheap.

headphone-fiio-jt3.review: The tonality is a bit sharp at 8 kHz, with high upper mids, and the mid-bass to sub-bass is higher than the JT7: more V-shaped, so to speak. But I like the fit, and I really like the price: only 1 million. Paired with a dongle it's still a bit hard to drive, but a SnowSky Melody works; then EQ it (my EQ is at the far right). A proper soundstage for 1 million, a bit held back on a dongle. The dilemma: it's cheap, so recommending a desktop DAC/amp like the DX5 II feels outrageous budget-wise, right? Try the Melody and EQ. High gain!

headphone-fiio-jt1.review: We're not sure if it's open, closed or semi-open, but it's surely a very well-tuned neutral headphone, with great vocals. The bass isn't boomy or even boosted. Very comparable to the SHP9500 in tuning, with less bright upper mids.

headphone-phillips-shp9500.review: If you're just starting to try OPEN-BACK headphones, many people recommend the SHP9500, and audiophiles respect it a lot as an entry-level open-back. Mid-centric.

headphone-sennheiser-hd25.review: A good driver, closed-back, but muddy with a lot of mid-bass/low-mids, and the sub-bass rolls off; similar to the KPH40 there, but brighter at 10 kHz. You can EQ it now that the SnowSky Tiny exists, so I treat it like having this headphone with a USB-C end whose EQ I can correct into something really goood. On-ear life changed since the SnowSky Tiny, lol. But it really is very expensive compared with the KPH40's value. The KPH's trick is that it's semi-open: more spacious after EQ. The HD25's cable exits upward, which is unique, and the left earcup can flip forward so it's like wearing one side only. Good for DJing.

headphone-koss-kph40.review: They are better than they look, and literally an OPEN-BACK design; the sound is amazing. It needs a bit more power. I had it customised to MMCX at Herz Garage (Tokopedia) to make it detachable, and swapping the cable helped a fair bit, especially 4.4 mm, which carries more power. Wide, open sound, a bit muddy with a lot of bass around 125 Hz; cut it a little and it's spot on. A bit tiring over long sessions because it's on-ear, but they sound nice: balanced, with more mid-bass but open-sounding. I suggest buying a SnowSky Tiny to EQ it: insanely good after EQ with the SnowSky Tiny. (Review on his YouTube.)

headphone-moondrop-old-fashioned.review: Like a Koss KPH40 with big, thick Yaxi earpads, but with a more neutral, cleaner, less muddy tuning compared with the KPH40/Porta Pro. Pleasant, very enjoyable. Just EQ it and it's great: add some bass, lovely.

headphone-audio-technica-m40x.review: The main weakness of AT's M-series is that the HINGE, the bend at the driver, BREAKS VERY OFTEN. That's why I always recommend people go straight for the MDR-7506, DT770, or even the SHP9500 if they want open-back, because none of those break easily. Mate, you buy an expensive headphone and it breaks: sad. But I think the M40x's tuning is better than the M50x: just flatter.

headphone-audio-technica-m50x.review: The HINGE at the driver bend breaks easily. More fun-sounding than the M40x, but less flat as a result. The treble is a bit metallic to me; not metallic exactly: veiled, less natural. But it has more bass than the M40x, so it's more fun for monitoring. Even though my favourite band, Arctic Monkeys, used this for monitoring while recording Tranquility Base Hotel & Casino, I think you'd be better off buying the MDR-7506 all the way if it's fully for monitoring and enjoying music, and every MDR-7506 part is replaceable. But this one is also very suitable for listening to music and recording.

headphone-takstar-pro-82.review: Good, balanced, very neutral. Not stinging, nothing weird. Plugged straight into a sound card it's already nice. Comes with a nice hard case. Crazy, I only just learned about this; I tried it at an audio meetup and the value turns out to be excellent.

headphone-isk-hd-9999.review: One of the headphones with a flat, neutral tuning for mixing too, though there's a slight early bump after 200 Hz. Pamungkas's audio engineer uses this headphone for mixing (see their video), and just listen: Pamungkas's mixes, live and studio, are all good, right?

headphone-pioneer-se-ms5t.review: Neutral leaning bright. The mid-bass punch comes through, down to the sub-bass actually. If only the earcup clamp were a bit tighter, it could be bassier. But neutral like this is already very nice. Good clarity, good resolution compared with buying cheap wireless headphones.

headphone-dbe-dj500.review: A local (Indonesian) neutral headphone. The sound is actually not bad, just a bit bright. I can't see a graph yet since it's a local headphone, and those rarely get measured, but it's fairly neutral. Unique accessories: a 6.5 mm input, a 3.5 mm input, and a mic cable too.

headphone-audio-technica-s120c.review: FINALLY, cheap wired on-ear headphones are back. This is really nice, even nicer than cheap 100–300k wireless ones. It can even rival the Sony CH520 at around 700k: very balanced! Detailed and clear, because it's wired. It ends in USB-C too, so it's very practical to use.

headphone-superlux-hd681.review: This sound leans neutral too and works well for mixing. Semi-open-back: it leaks a bit, but not as much as an open-back. Very enjoyable, and one of RTINGS' top 10 for value for money. A bit bright, but very open-sounding.

headphone-tascam-th-02.review: Recommended to me by Mas Ki when I worked at NET (the TV station). When going out on shoots they didn't want to bring expensive headphones, so they brought this one. Mid-frequency-centric. Not truly flat, but very helpful for mixing, especially vocals.

headphone-samson-sr850.review: This is kind of everybody's first headphone among people who mix. Honestly, you're better off with this than some no-name gaming brand. The fit is OK, and it's over-ear and very comfortable.
